newsitem.title: USA: Clinton far ahead in Midwest battleground - poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton far ahead in Midwest battleground - poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton leads Republican Bob Dole by 15 percentage points in a Reuters poll of sentiment across three key Midwestern battleground states where the presidential election could be decided.

The poll of 1325 likely voters in Ohio, Michigan and Illinois, conducted by John Zogby Group International and released on Wednesday, found Clinton ahead of Dole 47.3 percent to 32.2 percent in the overall three-state sampling. Ross Perot polled 4.4 percent and 15 percent were undecided.
The poll, conducted Sept. 13-16, carries a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points. The margin of error grows to plus or minus five points for each individual state.
Clinton's lead is widest in Michigan, where he is over 20 points ahead of Dole, 50 percent to 29.5 percent.
In Illinois, the president's advantage is about 16 points, 48.2 percent to 32.4 percent. The race is closest in Ohio, where Clinton leads by 13 points, 45.7 to 32.3 percent.

These three states alone carry 61 votes in the Electoral College, 22 percent of the 270 vote majority needed to be elected president. Many analysts believe Dole probably needs to carry two of the three states to win the Nov. 5 election.

"These are must-win states for Dole and he is much further behind than he should be at this stage of the campaign," said pollster John Zogby. "He has a lot of work to do to make this election competitive."

Clinton has double-digit leads among all age groups, both genders, among both women working outside the home and those not, people who have lost a job in the past year and those who have not, people afraid of losing a job in the next year and those not afraid, and people working at a job for less pay than a year ago and those not.
Clinton draws 82 percent of his own Democrats while Dole captures only 65 percent of the Republicans. Clinton's lead among independents is 41 percent to 24 percent.
But Dole leads among the region's 1992 Perot voters, 29 percent to Clinton's 24 percent and Perot's 24 percent.

In the key swing group of Catholic voters, Clinton leads 54 percent to 29 percent. Even among those calling themselves "born-again Christians", often among the most loyally Republican voters, Dole only leads by 45 to 35 percent.

In follow-up interviews with some of those who took part in the poll, many said they thought that, at 73, Dole was too old to be president. Others expressed doubts about his plan to cut income tax rates by 15 percent.

"Dole is OK but he's too old to run the country and he's too much of a backroom politician," said David Flamer, a technology consultant from Milford, Michigan, who said he would support Republicans in congressional elections but Clinton for the White House.
Beth Lewis, a homemaker in South Haven, Michigan, said: "Right now, I'm leaning to Clinton. He's more in tune with the generation coming up and the kind of education they will need to survive."

Carole Zoeller, a Chicago homemaker said: "Dole is a wonderful leader who has achieved a lot. He's just a little past the curve. It would have been wonderful if he had got the nomination a few years back." She intends to vote for Clinton.
Said Gary Bishop, a Grand Blanc, Michigan, auto worker who is leaning towards Perot: "Dole's 15 percent tax cut is just a fantasy to try to get elected."

Support for Democrats in Congress lags Clinton's backing by a considerable margin. By a narrow 37 percent to 35 percent, the region's voters say they will vote for the Democratic House of Representatives candidate in their district over the Republican.

Voters are split evenly on whether the country is heading in the right direct or wrong direction, but 53 percent think that Clinton deserves re-election. And by a narrow 38 percent to 35 percent, they favour Clinton's tax plan over Dole's.
